utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk as cases manager this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Annemarie McNulty appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do counsel have any preliminary matters to raise before we deal with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. It seems to me wholly unlikely that the witness will take the whole of this morning's hearings so there are a number of administrative matters which I've alerted the Defence to and I would like to raise when he is finished. And I hope Your Honours are aware of them. I did send an e-mail it to the Legal Officer. Or, rather, she was on the same e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a matter, because Ms. Korner will take it at the end of the session, I propose that I raise it as well at the end of the session so we can finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we go into closed session so the witness can be escorted into court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understood the witness didn't want protective measures any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber has to satisfy itself of that. So we are going to take this step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now that we are in open session, I repeat what I said a short while ago because the public is now able to hear the proceedings. They are still not able to recognise your face or identify your voice because of the existing protective measures which had been sought on your behalf and granted. Since that time, we have been informed that you no longer wish to have those protective measures in place. Would you be so kind as to confirm to the Chamber that this -- that our understanding -- whether our understanding is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has understood my application well. Let me explain. In August earlier this year when the investigators in Banja Luka told me that I was to appear in this trial and asked me if I wanted any protective measures, I expressed my wishes for protective measures on the spur of the moment. Later on as I gave it some thought, I concluded that I may have spoken hastily because there isn't anything that I would like to conceal from the public or that I would fear, and I would wish these protective measures to be rescinded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Chamber, therefore, makes the following order: During the proofing session of witness SZ-020, the witness present on the stand, it emerges that the witness decided he no longer needs any protective measures in order to testify, although he had previously had requested protective measures. In its decision of the 6th of December, 2011, the Chamber had granted him the use of pseudonym, image and voice distortion. In light of the fact that the witness has given his consent to testifying publicly, pursuant to Rule 75(K), the Trial Chamber rescinds the protective measures granted to him after duly noting the requirements of Rule 75(J). He will now be referred to by his name in the course of the trials and other related proceedings. And that order takes effect immediately. Thank you, usher. Would you please now hand the card to the witness so that he might make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may resume your seat. The solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to give evidence truthfully and should you fail to do so, this Chamber is -- this Tribunal is empowered by its statute and rules of procedure to impose the penalties for perjury, should you give false or misleading testimony. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nijaz Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, ethnicity, and present or former profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of June, 1954. Bosniak. Bosnian. Currently deputy director of the police, of the Ministry of the Interior therefore, of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in these cases, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have been called by counsel representing one of the two accused on trial before this Chamber, that is counsel for the accused Mr. Zupljanin. It is expected that your testimony will be completed by the time the -- by the time the Chamber rises for the day at 1.45 and counsel for Mr. Zupljanin will begin by asking you questions, then counsel for his co-accused will have an opportunity to cross-examine you, followed by counsel for the Prosecution, and then counsel calling you would have the right to re-examine. The Bench itself may at that stage or, indeed, at any earlier stage have -- also be able to ask questions and unless there's something -- some question which you have which I may be able to answer by way of explanation I would invite, counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, I think it's Mr. Krgovic, to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to the questions put to you by the Chamber, you gave us some personal background. Now I'd like to hear from you certain information about your professional background. What degrees do you have?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law and I graduated from the law school in Banja Luka in 1992 and I had some also undergraduate studies that I completed in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you began working for the police?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 1st of November, 1999 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, can you just repeat the year?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of November, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what were your initial duties in the police?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I started working as deputy commander of the police station charged with traffic safety in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever perform any other duties, and if so, which year was that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in that job until May of 1993, I believe. At that point I was inspector for crimes in traffic, infractions in traffic. And then in 1995 I worked as assistant commander of the police station charged with general duties. In other words, I moved from the traffic department to the general duty department, as it were, in Bosanska Gradiska. Subsequently, in 1999 in the spring of 1999, always in the same station, I became deputy commander of the general duty police station where I stayed until June of 2001 when I was assigned to be assistant commander of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, and that was until 2003, and in that same centre, I became deputy chief of a public security centre. That was until October of 2004 when I became chief of the police administration of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. Last year I was chosen and selected as -- to be deputy director of the police of the MUP of Republika Srpska in a public competition and that's the duty that I'm currently performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One clarification. In reference to 2001 there's the Security Services Centre mentioned in Banja Luka. What was it called in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know which year was it renamed public security centre?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the war-time period?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, several years after the war it must have been. At the time when state security was taken out of the organisation of the Ministry of the Interior by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smajlovic, or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be given a hard copy of his statement because I wanted to elicit certain clarifications. And can we call up in e-court 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not clear on the basis in which the witness can just have his statement in front of him. He has been called live, I understand it. Not 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he is called as a 92 bis witness and I'd like him to clarify certain issues that he gave in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, he is not a 92 bis witness. He is a 92 bis -- you applied for 92 bis, he was ordered to be called. I mean, I don't have any strong feelings, Your Honour, but at the moment it's my view that as the witness is giving evidence live, he should give his evidence and not just have his statement, but it's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, this witness has been called as a 92 ter witness, so I should actually ask him if he would give the same answers if asked the same questions, so he has to confirm his statement, that's why I misunderstood what Ms. Korner had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Krgovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 8D2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were able to have a look at this statement. Is that the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by the statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will have several questions for you. Can you tell me, when was it the first time that Stojan Zupljanin's Defence got in touch with you with a view to you giving your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It was in January earlier this year that I was first contacted by investigators in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who contacted you specifically?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mirko Bojnovic, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Bojnovic have to ask of you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he told me the commonly known fact that there's a trial against Stojan Zupljanin conducted here and that in 1991, 1992, 1993 when I used to work in the police station in Bosanska Gradiska, he was performing his duties and he wanted to know if we had ever been in any dealings formerly, at various meetings, and my answer was affirmative, that, yes, as assistant commander, I attended these meetings. Therefore, he asked if I would be willing to testify about his character as it were and his treatment of the various employees of the MUP and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did Zupljanin's Defence contact you next?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in late January or early February of this year. As agreed with investigators, a written statement was drawn up. It's the statement that is before me now. And I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given a chance to review the statement at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My words were translated into this written statement. I read it and signed it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then confirm or authenticate the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by affixing my signature. It happened in late March and it does say here specifically on the 22nd of March that a lady arrived from The Hague, from this Tribunal, in other words, and it was in her presence that I authenticated the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you then again contacted by the Defence for Stojan Zupljanin in the course of the summer?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in July we had another meeting where I was told that the Prosecution of this Tribunal found my statement interesting and that they would like to get in touch with me on these issues. I inquired and was told that it was up to me to decide freely if I wanted to meet up with them, and then under those circumstances, I decided that I would not get in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did investigators of the Zupljanin Defence get in touch with you at a later date concerning protective measures?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In August I was told that I would have to appear before the Chamber in person, and that I could opt for protective measures, which I chose at the time. Though, as I say, subsequently I realised that there was no need for that because I don't have to hide behind my statement. And it was in August, I think, that a written statement on these issues was made, or a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the investigator made a note of this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that were you contacted by the Zupljanin Defence in this autumn concerning your interview to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in early October I was on a business trip and it so happened that I was in the Netherlands but I had to return and couldn't do it then. Upon my return I asked Mr. Bojnovic what this was about and he told me that the OTP insisted on interviewing me, but since I wasn't obliged to agree, I declined. There was an official note made about this and the next thing that happened was the summons to come here on the 15th or the 16th so that nothing in writing was ever produced because of the shortage of time, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in The Hague, did you talk to me the day before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the day when I arrived, on Monday, you again pointed out this possibility to me and I can only repeat I don't consider it very important and I declined once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask whether you should meet the Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, you told me that the Stanisic Defence also wanted to talk to me and I declined again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smajlovic, in your statement you mention the structure, or rather, the ethnic composition of the Gradiska police station. And in paragraph 3 you gave the details, so I need not go into that. But I would like to clarify something. Do tell us before that when you arrived, it was noted here that you arrived on Monday. When did you really arrive?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I am sorry, it was Wednesday. On Monday I was contacted by somebody from The Hague and I left on Wednesday and arrived on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were speaking about the ethnic composition of the police in April 1992. Did the ethnic composition of the MUP change? Did any colleagues of other ethnicities leave? I'm not interested in a very detailed account but only whether there was a change in the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: At the traffic police station there were some 26 to 28 officers, including the senior officers. There were very few non-Serbs but I was one. There were three more police officers, so that would make a total of four. Throughout these ugly events, I mean the war, one more police officer remained and in the meantime people were leaving. If you are asking about the overall ethnic makeup of the police in Gradiska, including the general duty police station which has the premise -- its premises in the same building and has jurisdiction in the Gradiska municipality, I am not sure how many non-Serb officers there were, but maybe up to 20 per cent according to my estimate. And the total number of police officers of that station was around 60. Certainly during the year that number dwindled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 you speak about Mr. Zupljanin. These meetings, collegiums or whatever they were called, when did you begin to attend these meetings and during which period and until which time did you go there?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. I said that I began to work for the police on the 1st of November, 1990 as deputy commander. A police station is headed by the commander. Whenever a commander for any reason cannot do something, it is my duty as deputy to step in. If you are asking me about the meetings of the senior officers of the security services, in 1991 I went to these meetings too and in 1992 not more than twice. It was in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The event you described when Mr. Zupljanin spoke to you and told you that nobody must harm you, was it before or after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that must have been in late April 1992. There was a meeting about the general security situation and other technical matters. This was an informal conversation after a meeting. The then chief of the public security station, Mr. Vesic, was also present. The statement was Mr. Zupljanin's reaction to my conduct in the police and everything I was saying when the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being established, which today is the MUP of the RS. I don't know if a more detailed explanation is required, what kind of conversations these were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us what kind of conversation did you have in the field or at the station?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that day - I'm not sure about the date - there was a meeting of all public security staff in Gradiska, and we were informed that I think as of the 1st of April, 1992, and the meeting was immediately after that, a decision was passed to establish the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was a consequence of political events and talks in Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond about the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its people. And since everything functioned, everything worked. The authorities both at municipal level and in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the first significant changes were those in the police. My attitude and what I also stated publicly was that we, in Gradiska, should not divide along ethnic lines because if that happened unwanted consequences would probably come about as we were -- had already been able to see in some parts of Eastern Bosnia. And I was appealing to my friends, neighbours, and everybody who lived in town to behave accordingly. The leadership of the station gave the choice to everybody in the station, Serbs and non-Serbs alike, what they would opt for. We were still wearing the red star on our uniform hats and the only change at that moment was to substitute that red star with the colours of Republika Srpska. And all staff were given ten days or so whether they would accept that or not, and the regulations required us to give a solemn declaration to continue working for the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's much like the one I made this morning. And that was it. After that the commander of the police station, the general duty police station, Dragoljub Novakovic and the commander of the traffic police station where I worked, Momir Topic, and I as his deputy, and the general duty police station didn't have a deputy at the time. The three of us, in agreement with the chief of the station, Vesic, had made a plan to talk to our staff, especially non-Serbs, and ask them to remain in the police because it's never too late for divisions and problems. We tried to calm down the situation and wanted to avoid the citizens of Gradiska, irrespective of their ethnicity, to feel unsafe, and that's what we did. We talked to people, sometimes they did it on their own, sometimes I did it on their own and sometimes we did it together. And those were all fair conversations. Some staff remained, others didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you talk to these people to ask them to stay with the police?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I went to see some five or six at their homes and with others I talked to at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any pressures on these people to leave the MUP of the RS?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I never cared much for politics. I never sided with any party. Although the police wasn't allowed to affiliate itself politically, I still don't know who had sympathy for who.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions of this witness. Your Honours, I would just like to tender this statement after the OTP's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No cross-examination for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When Mr. Bojnovic came to speak to you, was he somebody you knew from the time when he worked for the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Bojnovic when I began to work at the CSB, which means in 2001 or 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Bojnovic explain to you why he had come to see you? Why you in particular, to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't explain much. I've just told you when I first met him. At the time he was chief of one of the departments. In our official and private contacts we probably spoke about the time before the war and it is possible that he came to see me due to these conversations that we had had before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any direct contact by telephone with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hesitate at all before you agreed to give evidence about Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hesitate at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why? Is that a because he was a good friend of yours or because he protected you during the war, or for whatever other reason?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin was chief of the centre which means that he was not a friend of mine. We didn't know each other personally. We had official contacts. He had a register of his people in the field and he may have noticed me at one of the meetings. When he said what he said, I don't think that he would have recognised me on that occasion. He was actually talking to Mr. Vesic, but given the opportunity I introduced myself. However, there is -- we don't really know each other directly, either privately or officially, because I was one of many senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The reason -- I'll explain why I'm asking you whether you hesitated. You come from Sanski Most, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Sanski Most was one of the areas which came under the area of responsibility of the CSB Banja Luka in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you spent your whole life since 1990 in the police. Are you saying you didn't realise that Sanski Most comes within the area of responsibility of the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Ms. Korner please specify the period she is referring to in her question. She did say 1992 earlier on but is 1992 still the period referred to in the second question because there were changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I really would be grateful if I didn't have objections such as this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I'll repeat the question. You are aware, aren't you, fully, that in 1992 Sanski Most came under the responsibility, the authority, of the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: In 1978 I left Sanski Most and have since lived in Gradiska. I was a football player. I lived there with my wife and family until 2001 or 2002 when I moved to Banja Luka. I got a job there. The fact that I was born in Sanski Most has nothing to do with my professional work, I believe. That's why I gave this answer. I have links with Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. When you attended meetings, as you've told the Court you did, up until about May of 1992 at the CSB Banja Luka, and that's how you met Mr. Zupljanin, were you not aware that at these collegiums the representatives of Sanski Most were attending as well?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Those were meetings at which 50 to 60 people were present. The invitation to a meeting only came to the organisational unit that was to respond. That's why I don't see any problem with my statement. I said I think so, but I might as well say, yes. But I did not know the people from the field who belonged to other organisational units, so that is who were from other towns. Until 1990, I did something else altogether. In late 1990, I joined the police force and I literally had no time to get acquainted even with the hierarchy in traffic safety, let alone the personnel structure in other municipalities. The centre covered Bosanska Krajina, which is an extensive area, with many organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When the investigator came to see you about whether you want protective measures -- wanted protective measures in August, you told him, didn't you, that you were born in Sanski Most, you still owned property in Sanski Most, and you go there occasionally to visit family and friends; is that right? Was that a correct statement by you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I have two sisters and a brother in Sanski Most and my wife's family is there, and it's true that I go there occasionally. Well, simply speaking, you know, I took a decision rashly but why back out now because I think that it isn't important in the least because there's no danger to me or my immediate or extended family. I could have stayed but there are no problems, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not at the moment dealing with why you wanted the protective measures rescinded. I'm simply dealing with you and your knowledge of Sanski Most. You are, are you not, I aware of what happened to your Muslim and non-Serb colleagues generally in Sanski Most in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really? You've not heard about any of the events that took place in Sanski Most in 1992? Is that what you are telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. That is, in 1992 and so on I didn't have such contacts. After the war, yes, informal -- or through informal conversations, but I have a very superficial knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really. So you know nothing about Bajtonika [sic], is that what you are saying? It's no good looking at counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last thing you said was not interpreted. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I saw him looking over as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you telling the Court, sir, you know nothing about Bajtonika, the prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Betonirka prison, Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was trying to be helpful because I see that the interpreters didn't understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well I'm surprised after all this time and the number of times I've said it, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, is that what you are telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I can say to this Trial Chamber that my contacts with the citizens of Sanski Most are limited to my family. My relatives, close or distant, didn't go to Betonirka and I personally never investigated, privately or officially. And for your information, I only went to Sanski Most around 2000 after the war. All my family had lived abroad from before the war in Germany, Switzerland, and a number -- or more specifically, a sister and a brother of the six of us also left Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. And my wife's family did as well. And there was no need for me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, it may be there was no need for you, but I'm asking you as a matter of record, are you telling the Court that you are unaware of the shelling of M ahala in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I am unaware. You can believe me. At the time in 1992, the phone lines between towns and municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were disrupted. I'm talking to you about my feelings and my experience. My mother was in Sanski Most at the time and so was my brother and my sister and my wife's family and I couldn't contact them, or only very rarely. And I don't even remember how we managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: And when they were leaving --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not asking -- I'm now asking you whether you are telling the Court that after the end of the conflict, you heard nothing about the events that happened in Sanski Most as it affected the non-Serb population? Is that what you are telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to say that I first went there, to Sanski Most that is, five or six years later and we didn't discuss these things then. The people I talked to then -- well, and finally, it isn't anything that I take interest in. I didn't feel it or experience it the way you are trying to present it. I lived in Gradiska with my family, with my wife and children, with my neighbours and friends and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason I've been asking you about this is going back to my original question, whether you felt any hesitation in testifying on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin who was in charge of the police area in Sanski Most, and you told me you didn't, so none of these events, you say you knew about?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin was not just in charge of Sanski Most. He was the chief of the centre that covered a large geographic area, including Bosanska Gradiska where I was working. What I know, what I saw, what I felt, what I heard at meetings, that means objectively and anything that I was told directly, the reaction I had to this was as such, and, therefore, I did not hesitate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you declined when you were asked to speak to the Prosecution as a high-ranking member of the Republika Srpska police?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I did so because I didn't have the need to do that. It was not obligatory, I didn't want to dwell on years that I don't want to remember. I don't want to relive the stress just as I'm now. You are asking very problematic questions that I have nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you were going to relive the stress by giving the evidence that you gave to the Defence and I'm asking you why you didn't want to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: A smaller dose of stress then talking to the Defence [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of your superiors in the Republika Srpska police, for example, Mr. Milosevic, about whether you should refuse to speak to the Prosecution? Or Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic is not my superior, if you are talking about Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I am the deputy director and he is my superior. As with Mr. Vasic, to, certainly not, there was no need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you knew that Mr. Vasic had testified here, didn't you, in this trial?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he -- did you know -- did you ask him whether he had spoken to both the Prosecution and the Defence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you never took any advice on this at all?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't think there was any need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you had no reason, other than you say, stress for not wishing to speak to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No other reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see there's an apparent conflict between the answer at 10 and 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said first of all -- 8, sorry 10. You said Mr. Milosevic was not your superior and then you went on to say if you are talking about Dragomir Milosevic, I'm the deputy director and he is my superior. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: He is not the superior, I'm not talking about Drago but Dragomir, I don't know how it was interpreted that it was said that Drago Milosevic is the deputy chief of the police and I am the deputy director and my position is above the chief of crime police or deputy chief of police, not underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So the reality is that from 1992 until today the whole of your police career has been spent in the Republika Srpska police? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to look at some of the events in Bosanska Gradiska now, to give the context of your remaining with the police during this period. Can we first of all establish, let's have a look at the map, exactly where Gradiska is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, 10137.1. And it's tab 16 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Gradiska is the border municipality, is it not, if one looks, one focuses where Banja Luka is, if we can, yes, go in a bit there. Thank you. Bosanska Gradiska is right on the border with Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed still has one of the major crossings from Bosnia into Croatia; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we see Banja Luka, the town, and the municipality, and on the other side Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Bosanska Dubica. Right, now, let's look at the ethnic makeup, please, of Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. This is a character witness and the Prosecution now wants to talk about ethnic composition of Bosanska Gradiska and this is not the subject of -- this is a wide-ranging line of questioning and as far as I understood the Court, the Prosecution can ask character questions of the witness and not to present evidence and not to ask him about things in Bosanska Gradiska that have nothing to do with this indictment. I think this should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it has nothing to do with this indictment. However, there are two things. First of all, the witness has gone beyond character in his account of the break-up of the police in Bosanska Gradiska. Second, it is not possible, we would submit, to assess the credibility of the evidence this witness is going to give without looking at the background of the events to which he was a party. And the fact that the Defence have decided to call this witness purely for character, but as I say going further, is not the point. In any event, the assessment Your Honours have to make has to be based on the evidence that there is surrounding his testimony. I didn't propose to belabour this but I'm entitled to do this in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I seem to recall us having to rule on a like objection probably in the last setting whereas the -- under the -- the rules with which Ms. Korner and I would be familiar that cross-examination is at large does not really apply at the Tribunal in that cross-examination is not confined but certainly must relate to the evidence led in chief. But on the other hand, the matters which obviously touch on the witness's credibility or ability, really, to give evidence on which the Chamber must place reliance, that leeway must be allowed. So provided Ms. Korner so confines herself, I see no objection -- no reason not to permit her to proceed along that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have up, please, 65 ter 20376. Can we just, please, highlight the breakdown of the population that we can see at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bosanska Gradiska was an overwhelmingly Serb municipality - wasn't it? - had a total majority over any of the other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: You are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Were you aware of those figures?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I must say in the system in which I lived, in which all of us lived, and the education we had at home or generally did not focus us on these figures and these figures didn't mean anything to ordinary people. They didn't mean anything to me. I don't feel even today, not to say then, who was who or divisions as to who belongs to what group as stated here. So believe me, these numbers, I did not know these numbers at that time. Later, of course, after what we went through, had we wanted to or not, just from general information and all the suffering we went through and the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war that lasts even today where people want to group themselves into various groups, I know these, but at the time in 1991, 1992, when things began, nobody was thinking about this, at least I was not thinking about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may not personally, but I can assure you, sir, numbers of people are able to quote these figures. But, however, do you accept that Bosanska Gradiska, this is the 1991 census, had an overwhelming majority of Serb population, people who declared themselves to be Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I accept this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But there were some 15.000 odd Muslims and 3.000 odd Croats. Do those figures sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir. You told us you'd been in Gradiska from 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It's all right. As I said, I didn't deal with these things but it's an official census and it certainly must have been like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it's right, isn't it, sir, that from the outbreak of the conflict in Croatia itself, there were problems starting, because Gradiska is so close to the border, against other ethnicities, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I must say this: I worked at the traffic security police station. As far as matters such as these are concerned and verification of such information, I cannot answer them with yes or no or make certain claims. I will try to contribute and try to answer from my general knowledge. Of course, I lived in Gradiska and had family and friends there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, I am going to stop you, sir. I'm going to ask you about specific events and matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, now, on the screen, document 20380.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You knew who Bishop Komarica was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, tab 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about Bishop Komarica from the period after the war, but before the war, no, no, I didn't know who he was, what his -- what religious dignitary function this had. I know of him from after the war. Believe me, the time up to the was, the beginning of the war, as things heated up, I simply was not interested in this area. I did not know religious dignitaries, any others, or those of a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to consider this: This is a letter from him addressed to the chief, Mr. Vesic of your SJB. And he is complaining in February of 1992 about attacks on nuns in Nova Topola. Do you know where Nova Topola is?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did your chief Mr. Vesic tell you that apparently members of the Catholic religious orders were being attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: My chief, Mr. Vesic, the chief -- organisationally, he was not my chief, my immediate superior was Commander Momir Topic. Functionally, Commander Momir Topic was connected with the SJB, specifically to the police sector. At the head of the sector was Mr. Stevan Markovic, the late Stevan Markovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I'm going to stop you, we all want to finish as soon as we can today. I really asked you a very simple question to he which the answer is either yes or no. Did Mr. Vesic at any stage --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on then shall we.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I had to -- I had to explain because you said your superior Vesic and this is why I gave this explanation. The answer in connection with this specific document is no, he didn't have the need to do so nor was I in charge of security of this type in Bosanska Gradiska municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's continue to what started to happen after the outbreak of the conflict. Could you have a look, please, at a report on the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the number is, it's at tab 3, and it's 2 -- 65 ter 20371.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting for one moment, sir, that you had ever seen a report like this but I want to ask you about the incident that's described in there. And paragraph 3, we can bring that up, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have to go to the next page, I think, in B/C/S. Could we go to the next page in B/C/S because we can see it in English but not B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see that they are recording on the 21st of April: "In Bosanska Gradiska citizens of Muslim ethnicity started assembling in the evening hours of the 20th of April, but the gathering broke up quietly after the police intervened." Do you recall gatherings -- a gathering of Muslims being broken up by the police very early on in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's right, isn't it, that the Muslims in Bosanska Gradiska posed absolutely no threat to anybody?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. None of the ethnic groups represented any type of threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what happened now. Now, let's look, please, at the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, P367. Tab 4. Sorry, wrong -- I'm so sorry, wrong one, my fault, it's tab 4, 65 ter 10006.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Bosanska Gradiska had a Territorial Defence unit, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. Although, I don't understand these things. I don't understand military organisation. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Didn't you do military service, sir, at some stage?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you are saying that your -- you think they had a Territorial Defence. Were you aware that the Territorial Defence that was being supplied arms by the Banja Luka corps, 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, it's still the 5th Corps. Now, let's consider what happened after that. A programme of disarmament went on, didn't it, of non-Serbs in Bosanska Gradiska from late May onwards? Sir? Did you hear the question? It's right, isn't it, sir, there was a programme of disarming the non-Serbs in Bosanska Gradiska which was being carried out by the police in Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear about the programme. I don't know about it. As far as disarming, yes, there was disarming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Disarming of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I say disarming. According to the laws in effect today and even then, military weapons cannot be in the possession of citizens, civilians. Within that context, we can view it officially for disarming, for taking away illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"] weapons, this was something that was done. This was done by the general police station, not the police station where I worked. I don't want to limit this only to Muslim citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We, well I'm going to show you a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, line 29/11 says "for taking away legal weapons". I don't think that that is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Line 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 29, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Line 11, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "For taking away legal weapons," I think he said something opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you say, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have this here, I have some kind of dispatch in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you say -- sorry, it's all right, I'll repeat the question. There seems to be a mistranslation. Did you say that there was officially a disarmament of taking away of legal weapons or illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Illegal, therefore, the police, the police workers of the general police took away illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What they were doing, sir, was taking away legally owned or taking away or making the owners hand in legally-owned hunting rifles, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. Possible. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sir, we are not talking -- Bosanska Gradiska SJB wasn't a huge SJB, was it? It was quite a small one.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that in your time working there full time, and I'll come back in a moment to how you came to be doing that, you heard nothing about the disarmament, the taking away of hunting rifles and the like from what were described, in the report I'll show you in a minute, as the Muslim and Croat, Croatian extremists?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, again if we look, please -- oh, I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Hunting rifles are being taken away even today. Who uses such weapons illegally even if he possesses them legally are taken away by various procedure whether criminal, misdemeanor, administrative. If these things did happen, then there was probably some kind of assessment of this and it was probably an administrative matter. What I want to tell you is that, yes, I lived there, but my position and the work I did, for which I was responsible, they cannot be brought into context with what you are asking about. These were difficult times, let me tell you, very difficult times. Everyone tried to protect himself, above all his family. Who did anything -- those who did anything illegal, it was their decision, it was up to them. They are the ones who will be held liable for this sooner or later. Please understand that my name, my position, my conduct, my life philosophy cannot be brought into this context. I had my own family and I took care to do my task professionally. And all of these terrible times that are now behind us, I want it to end and preserve our lives, preserve our friends and so on. Perhaps this is a bit broad but please understand, please understand the context of everything that happened. I want to tell you what I am saying was really like that. I was really not interested in anything except for what I was responsible before myself, before the people, before God.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you feel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Ms. -- Mr. Smajlovic, we are about to take a break. We have to break at intervals in order for the tapes to be changed. So we will continue your testimony in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to finish very quickly the topic -- [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two documents relating to the disarmament, please. The first is at tab 6 and is P411.29. Can we go, please, it's -- it's 1st Krajina Corps report of the 1st of June. Can we go to the third page in English, please, and the same in B/C/S. And it's the top part in English and B/C/S it's the beginning of the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The municipalities of Bosanska Gradiska" and then gives the other ones, "are stable..." pause there. Do you agree in June of 1992 the municipality was a stable one?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And "Muslim and Croatian extremists," as it's written here, "have started handing in their weapons." And do you agree that weapons were being collected from the Muslim and Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I did say population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, do you agree that the people being disarmed were not the Serbs, but the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that statement only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have a look, please, at another document on this topic which shows the list, and that's, please, the document at tab 11 which is 65 ter 20378. Sorry, yes, I have, 20374. 74, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know whether you saw that. It's an official dispatch from your SJB. Go to the last page, you'll see it's apparently signed by Mr. Vesic. And we see -- do you agree -- is that Mr. Vesic's signature?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, are you saying you never saw any signatures by him?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I, therefore, said I suppose so. Let me repeat, Vesic was not my immediate superior and I did not need to necessarily see his signature, but I did and this one appears to be his.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Vesic apparently replying to a request from the CSB about the weaponry seized, illegally procured or held. 36 automatic rifles and so on and so forth we can see. And the weapons were confiscated in the period from the 13th of July to the 20th of August and then at the bottom of page, licensing hunting weapons seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we need to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are hunting rifles, hunting carbines and sniping rifles. There's a long list. And it would appear that all of those were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The above weapons, do you see the paragraph, were confiscated from July to September for preventative and security reasons. Receipts were issued. We wish to point out we will send you information subsequently about an even larger quantity of hunting weapons confiscated in the same manner ... and then pistols. So it would appear that -- if we go down, sorry to the next paragraph short-barrelled weapons confiscated 1 September 1992, the same reason, for licensing hunting weapons. When we say the 1st of September, 1992 we mean that the operation of confiscating weapons is still underway, continue to inform the centre as there are a large number of weapons registered owned by Croat or Muslims. Do you agree, sir, that it would appear that certainly until the end of September there was a disarmament operation going on in respect of Muslims and Croats in Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I truly cannot remember from which date to which date it went on. Yes, there was this activity and weapons were taken off the population but I can't speak to the details. It's been 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see there's no mention of any illegally-owned weapons being taken off Serbs in this document, is there.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't yet even got to the point of reading who the weapons were seized off, if the document states that at all. Is there any mention of ethnicity at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I've just read you the paragraph: "... as there are large numbers of weapons registered in the area of Gradiska public security station, owned by Croatian or Muslim citizens." Do you see that? It's the penultimate paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it now. Well, if that's what the document states, then I suppose that was the case. I suppose the person who signed the document was aware of what he was signing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to disarming the population, Muslims and Croats were removed, weren't they, from the jobs that they held during this period of time between May and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: They were not in the station where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, anybody who declined to take the -- to make the declaration was removed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Nobody was removed. I presume that those who failed to report to work would have their employment contracts terminated by law. Still today our legislation provides for a termination of employment where the incumbent fails to appear for work for up to -- for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at one your own reports from Gradiska, please. 13th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, tab 12, 3512. 65 ter 3512. This is all to do with the communications in Bosanska Gradiska. If we can go, please, to, in English page 2 and in B/C/S to page 2 as well. Second paragraph in B/C/S, the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During 1992 staff member Meho Kovacevic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am sorry, I can't find this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, it's the top, if you look at the second paragraph in your language.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's now disappeared entirely from the screen: "... left his position because he did not sign the pledge of loyalty and went abroad with his family." Most of the officers didn't sign, did they? Most of the non-Serbs? You were one of the very very few?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the number of non-Serb workers, I don't know if it was many or few. Everybody had the right to make their own decision. I explained my own choice at the start and, as I say, it proved correct. Those who have some sense in their mind would, of course, be in favour of not waging a war, and after all, for the past 15 or 16 years, Bosnia-Herzegovina is functioning, well, the way it is. Therefore, political choices made in respect of the political organisation for the future are taken by politicians. We were ordinary people and we had to make sure as human beings, neighbours, and citizens not to divide and to make sure that we stick together. Had this happened thousands upon thousands of people would not have been killed. Unfortunately, not all of us are of the same mind and, as I say, this specific decision had to be taken by each and every individual of his own free will and based on his own convictions, and they should not have gone in favour of divisions but Meho Kovacevic made his choice and followed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said they had to make that decision of their own free will. Did you personally have pressure put on you to sign the declaration by Mr. Vesic and other Serbs or, indeed, even Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you bring pressure to bear on the people you visited at their homes, the non-Serbs, to sign?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: A friendly conversation cannot be qualified as pressure; therefore, I did not exert any pressure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to look, please, at the document which is at tab 14, 20375. [Microphone not activated] Now this is a statement that was made --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was made to the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo in 1994. It's by a gentleman named Abid Jugo, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. He is a neighbour of mine. A friend. We were on visiting terms before the war and during the war all the way up to the time when he relocated to Visoko, he exchanged his home for a home there. I even visited him in Visoko when I was on a business trip to Sarajevo, and as of a few years ago, Abid Jugo went to live in Norway because his children are there, so I know the man very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Therefore, you have no reason to think that he would say things about you which were untrue?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's just go through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could move it up, please, in English. He gives the rough breakdown of the ethnicity. Then can we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, he describes the political events until Mr. Ivastanjin became president of the Municipal Assembly. Then he describes who the other government bodies were and that in the SDS. And can you see the bit that says: "The chief of the SUP in Bosanska Gradiska is Vladan Vesic who had been chief before the war and whose mandate was then extended by the SDS. Apart from him in the SUP there were the following extremists, Mr. Novakovic, the station commander; Dragoje Samardzija, a deputy commander; and Mr. Zivkovic; and also Mr. Polic." Then this: "In the police station there's also a certain Nijaz Smajlovic in Sanski Most who is carrying out the duty of deputy commander in the station and who still holds that duty. I heard that when the Serbs were taking over power, Smajlovic put pressure on the Muslims who were in the SUP." Was that true?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I was following closely and reading, I'm a bit taken aback by this. Some of the functions and positions he listed here are incorrect, but this term, "one Nijaz Smajlovic from Sanski Most," I don't know about English but in our language when you say one Mr. So and so, that would mean a certain person, that would mean somebody you didn't know, whereas he was a friend of mine, a neighbour. One whose house I would visit and he would visit mine. So I'm sure he would not have used this term one Nijaz or certain Nijaz. He told me he had problems when he arrived in Visoko and that was in 1994 from what was a Serb entity so what he must have been asked a great deal of questions and I know he had enormous difficulties, a year or more, before he could actually take possession of the house that he was supposed to live in. So I'm really taken aback by this because Abid, whom I know, if he were to come here, I am sure would not have said this. As the sentence stands, "certain Nijaz Smajlovic" tells me that somebody must have pushed him to give this sort of statement to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you the question again. Is it true, as he says, that you put pressure on people to remain?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is not true. I said that a moment ago. It's just that I am a bit distressed now that I've read this document, and I wonder if he was able to read what they made of his words. What I said that there had been were friendly conversations with people of Muslim ethnicity because I lived in a neighbourhood, now that I have to say it, where most of the population were Muslims. And there were questions asked as to why not everyone stayed behind when a certain number of non-Serb workers stayed behind, whereas a certain number left. And people realised at a later date that they perhaps lacked courage to do this and that and then questions were asked about why some people decided to leave and why not all of them stayed behind. Because you know that care was always taken of the ethnic makeup. It is still the case today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be the case today. I'm suggesting to you, I'm going to come on to that, that what when on in Gradiska in 1992, with your connivance, sir, I'm afraid to say, was ethnic cleansing. Can we just finish this statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may briefly just interrupt. Your Honours, I didn't want to object earlier before the witness gave his answer in order that I would not be coaching a witness or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the witness with his earphones off, if he doesn't speak English, please. Can we confirm, perhaps you can confirm whether the witness speaks English or understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Smajlovic, can you understand English? Sorry, yes. Can you understand spoken English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may take your headphones off again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this situation, Ms. Korner is producing a witness statement and challenging the witness credibility based on the statement of some third person, and we don't have the confirmation that this person actually gave this statement. How do we know that? Was it -- was this statement taken out of his own free will? Perhaps yes, perhaps not. Has the contents of the statement where what he actually said or perhaps somebody added some things, because we have heard a number of testimonies where the witnesses were saying that the officials of the Bosnia-Herzegovina have added certain qualifications or certain events in some of their statements. Now, if Your Honours will recall, during the -- during the Prosecutor's case, we wanted to show the -- we wanted to show to the witnesses the statements given by some of the -- of the persons who were detained or interviewed during the -- during the interviewing process, for example, in Prijedor and elsewhere. And then the opposition by the Office of the Prosecutor was that we cannot establish that these statements were given by their own free will. And that is precisely the same situation as over here. And that is why I have -- I have to object at this point that Ms. Korner uses these documents for these purposes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Zecevic, that I fully understand what you are saying in terms of weight of this document having regard to its remoteness from the witness. We are dealing with multiple levels of hearsay and if I were sitting in a common law court, I would have no hesitation about excluding the use of the document. But as I understand the more liberal rules of the Tribunal, Ms. Korner is entitled to use it in the manner that she is, but she would appreciate that the -- for the reasons that you have identified and I've just echoed, that there's only so far that this would go but it's left at the end of the day for argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say the objection and indeed what Your Honours just said is quite remarkable, if Your Honours will recall exactly that, we took objection to the statements coming from people who have been interviewed in Omarska and we said that we objected to it for a number of reasons and we received a ruling from Your Honours which I can get which admitted each and every one of those statements with the caveat that, later, Your Honours would give it such weight as they deserved given that the person hadn't turned up to explain the circumstances. I'm proposing to ask Your Honours on that very basis to admit this statement into evidence as an exhibit when I finish going through it. And, indeed, we even have here a close connection. It's the hearsay element that I find surprising, Your Honour, because he says he knows this man, whereas the witnesses doing these endless Omarska statements, where it will show, a goodly number of which were admitted by Your Honours in the teeth of our strong objections and an application for reconsideration on it, this is exactly as I say, as I warned at the time, what is good for the goose is equally good for the gander and so I'm putting it to the witness, I'm going to ask for it be admitted because he knows the man indeed at the end of my examination on it, on the same basis as the Omarska statements and others were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner, I'm personally relieved that my instinctive conforms to what we have, in fact, formally ruled. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have one comment to what Ms. Korner said about this being hearsay evidence. This is not even hearsay evidence because if you take a more careful look at what this man here states, he says I heard from so and so. So in other words, not the one giving the statement heard it but heard it for somebody else, so this is twice or three times removed from the one making the statement. This doesn't even fulfill the criteria for hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that is what our American friends call totem-pole hearsay. Yes, please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then lists -- sorry, you can put your earphones on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then lists the various people who were in charge of companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He asserts that Mr. Ivastanjin, Mr. Barac and others including Mr. Vesic, together with the JNA, Banja Luka corps specifically, fully armed the Serbian population during 1990 to 1991, and, indeed, the SDS then carried out training. And deals with the weapons. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never heard anything about the SDS, the Banja Luka corps, and arming Serbs in Gradiska at all?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know --just departing for a moment from the statement - did you know a police officer in the SUP called Husret Mujadic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The SJB in Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have such one there as far as I remember. I don't know if a man by that name ever worked at that station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was there ever a time when members of the SJB were sent to attend, whilst you were there, courses in Belgrade before the conflict broke out on explosive devices, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of anybody being sent to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just finish then, please, with the statement that was made by this gentleman. He goes on to describe the crime that was committed in August of 1992. And do you remember when there was an incident where members of either the -- they were called the Skorpions or something to do with the police were actually killed by the other side, either Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: There were no Skorpions members in the police, nor were any police officers killed in August. But maybe you are referring to the events on the 8th and 9th of August. They involved army members, I think. There was a Gradiska Brigade, or whatever it was called. It was an incident when 16 young men were killed. They were from Gradiska. So this is not about the police but about army members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly the incident I'm referring to and I'll come back to that but I just want to complete this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 5 in English, and I think it is in page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there he says: "The torture and persecution of Muslims and Croats started when the war broke out. The main terror was carried out by the police, the so-called Serbian SUP headed by the chief Vladan Vesic and Ostoja Novakovic the commander of the police station. By Zivko Zivkovic, Drago Samardzija, the chief of the SUP formed a group of policemen led by the policeman Nikic who was the body-guard of the SUP chief." Now, before I go on to what is alleged here, were all these men that he names members of the SJB during 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Some information is wrong. Vladan Vesic was chief of the SJB but this also mentions Ostoja Novakovic, the commander of the police station but it's not Ostoja, it's Dragoljub Novakovic. Ostoja was the name of an assistant, but Ostoja Balaban. Zivkovic was a chief of the crime police department and not an inspector at the time. And Samardzija did not have an executive function at the station then, I think. And down there policeman Nikic but I'm fully certain that there was no police officer by that name. You said it was a small station and it was, but I don't know anybody by the name of Nikic. And especially since this states that he was a body-guard of the SUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. They go on to say: "During this day the group searched the homes of the Muslims and Croats because they were allegedly looking for weapons and at night the same houses and flats would be looted, set on fire, and mined. Some people were killed and some were taken to prison." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Or, actually, I cannot join in this. I'm unaware of such information. It certainly was not this way. I don't know where this gentleman, my neighbour and friend, got this from. I really couldn't say. I tried to read as much as possible from this document during the break but you need a major organisational unit to collect this amount of information. I don't know how he could have done that himself. I'm convinced that all these things were put in his mouth for him to simply sign off. I totally disagree with what he says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you watch the case against Radoslav Brdjanin at all, any of the court proceedings there?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so. But the reports are very concise. I don't think I followed Brdjanin, I did watch some though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, but -- so you weren't aware that your municipality, Bosanska Gradiska formed part of that case and that evidence was led about what happened there? You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that no one, to your knowledge, was arrested, brought to the police station, and then beaten up while they were being questioned?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: There were arrests, people were brought in, but about the treatment, I cannot comment. You are putting to me that people were being beaten and who knows what but I, personally, wasn't present, haven't seen anything, haven't heard anything and wasn't responsible for it. Neither me nor my organisational unit were not involved in such actions and I cannot confirm any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at a bit more of what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 6 in English, and it's the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I asked you earlier about the outbreak of war in Croatia. Did, as he allege, criminals come into Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ SMAJLOVIC
utterances.text: From where? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From -- Serbs from Croatia? Martic's men? The Krajina.
